header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |

The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.

This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
- `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
- `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.

<skill_resources>

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

lines.text: "title": "User passwords are stored and compared in plaintext",

"evidence": "addUser() (app/data/user-dao.js lines 17-31) builds the MongoDB user document directly from the signup form's password field with no hashing; the commented-out line 29 `password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` shows the hashing call exists in the codebase but is disabled. usersCol.insert(user, ...) then persists this raw value. validateLogin()'s comparePassword helper at line 61 (`return fromDB === fromUser;`) does a direct string equality check against the stored value, which only works if the stored value is the plaintext password, confirming nothing in the active code path ever hashes it. bcrypt-nodejs is imported at line 1 but its hashing/compare functions are never invoked.",

"impact": "Anyone who can read the users collection (a database compromise, an unrestricted backup, an operator with DB access, or any NoSQL-injection/IDOR bug elsewhere in the app) recovers every user's real password in clear text, which typically also compromises those users' accounts on other sites through password reuse.",
"fix": "Hash passwords with bcrypt (or argon2id) at signup using a modern cost factor, store only the hash, and compare with bcrypt.compare()/argon2.verify() in validateLogin instead of ===.",
"title": "Session cookie signing secret is a hard-coded literal in the committed configuration",

"evidence": "config/env/all.js exports this literal as `cookieSecret`, and config/config.js merges it unchanged into the exported config object (no environment-variable override exists for it, unlike port/db). server.js line 17 destructures `cookieSecret` from that config and server.js line 82 passes it straight into `session({ secret: cookieSecret, ... })`, the value express-session uses to sign and verify the session-id cookie.",

"impact": "The secret is public in the (open-source) repository and identical across every deployment that does not override it. Anyone who reads the source can compute a validly-signed session cookie for any userId, including admin accounts, and authenticate as that user without credentials.",
"fix": "Read cookieSecret from a required environment variable with no hard-coded fallback, generate it with a CSPRNG per deployment, and rotate the committed value.",
"title": "Encryption key for PII fields is hard-coded in the committed configuration",

"evidence": "config/env/all.js exports this literal `cryptoKey` alongside `cryptoAlgo: \"aes256\"`. app/data/profile-dao.js lines 18-39 (currently commented out) show the intended use: `crypto.createCipheriv(config.cryptoAlgo, config.cryptoKey, config.iv)` to encrypt ssn/dob before storage. That encryption path is disabled today (see the CWE-311 finding below), so this key is currently unused, but it is still a committed, shared secret that would defeat the encryption the moment that code path is re-enabled without rotating the key.",

"impact": "If the commented-out encryption code is turned back on without changing this key, every deployment shares the same encryption key from the public repository, letting anyone who has read the source decrypt any SSN/DOB stored under it.",
"fix": "Never commit encryption keys; load cryptoKey from a secrets manager or environment variable and rotate the value before enabling the encryption path.",
"title": "Full application configuration, including the session and crypto secrets, is logged to stdout on every startup",

"evidence": "`config` on line 10 is the merged object `{ ...allConf, ...envConf }`, which includes `cookieSecret`, `cryptoKey` and the MongoDB connection string `db` (which carries the DB credentials when MONGODB_URI includes a username:password, as it does on most non-local deployments). `util.inspect(config, false, null)` recursively stringifies the entire object with no redaction, and this module runs at require-time for every process start (server.js, artifacts/db-reset.js, and the test suite all require config/config.js).",

"impact": "Every process log — console output captured by Docker, Heroku's logging, or any log aggregator the operator ships stdout to — contains the session-signing secret and the database connection string in clear text, readable by anyone with log access even if they have no direct database or source access.",
"fix": "Remove the console.log of the full config, or log an explicit allowlist of non-secret fields (e.g. port, hostName) instead of the whole object.",
"title": "The application only ever listens on plain HTTP; the HTTPS setup is fully disabled",

"evidence": "server.js starts the app with Node's `http` module only. The alternative `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app)` block that reads artifacts/cert/server.key and server.crt is present but entirely commented out (lines 18-28 and 149-155), and there is no redirect from HTTP to HTTPS anywhere in the route table (app/routes/index.js). Every request this server handles — the login POST with userName/password (app/routes/session.js line 53-58), the session cookie set from that secret, and the profile POST with ssn/dob/bankAcc/bankRouting (app/routes/profile.js line 40-50) — therefore travels as clear text.",

"impact": "Anyone able to observe network traffic between the client and this server (a shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an on-path proxy) can read login credentials, the session cookie, and SSN/bank account/routing numbers as they are submitted.",

"fix": "Terminate TLS (uncomment and configure the existing https.createServer block or put the app behind a TLS-terminating proxy) and redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS; add Strict-Transport-Security once TLS is enforced.",
"title": "SSN and date of birth are written to the database unencrypted; the encryption code exists but is disabled",

Lines 12-13 then serialize the whole merged object with util.inspect and write it to stdout unconditionally, on every module load, i.e. every server start in every environment (development, test, and production alike, since config/env/production.js exports {} and does not disable this). No rate limiter is mounted anywhere in server.js to bound the rate of new sessions.",
45:     "impact": "An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly request any public route (e.g. \"/\") to make the Node process allocate one MemoryStore entry per request indefinitely, exhausting server memory and crashing the process for every user of the application - a remote, unauthenticated denial of service.",
46:     "fix": "Configure a bounded, shared session store with TTL-based eviction (e.g. connect-redis, connect-mongo) instead of the default MemoryStore, set saveUninitialized: false so anonymous visits do not create a stored session, and set an explicit cookie.maxAge.",

"impact": "Any network intermediary (shared Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an ISP) can read login credentials and the session cookie in transit and hijack any session or replay the credentials.",

"title": "Session cookie is issued with no httpOnly, secure or sameSite flag and the default cookie name",

"impact": "Because the cookie is not HttpOnly, any script-injection bug in the app (the templating engine's autoescape is also disabled, see the autoescape finding) can read `document.cookie` and exfiltrate the session id; because it is not Secure, the cookie is also sent over the plain-HTTP listener at server.js:145; the default `connect.sid` name additionally fingerprints the framework to an attacker.",
"fix": "Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: <a bounded value> }` and a non-default `name` on the session() call.",
"title": "No security-header middleware (helmet) is mounted; CSP, frame options, HSTS and MIME-sniffing protection are absent",

1: # Access department report — authentication, session handling and authorization
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/root/targets/NodeGoat` (OWASP NodeGoat), locked to the SHA-256 in `target.json` (111 files covered, minus `.git`). The tree is read-only; nothing in it was modified.
6: 
7: Method followed [review-method](../review-method): the route table was built first from `app/routes/index.js` (the only place `app.get`/`app.post`/`app.use` are called for application routes, plus the `/tutorial` router it mounts), then each route's middleware chain was read in full — `isLoggedIn` and `isAdmin` are both defined in `app/routes/session.js`, so both were read before judging any route "protected". Session configuration was read in `server.js` end to end, including every commented-out block, since a commented-out fix is direct evidence of what the maintainers knew was missing. Password handling was read in `app/data/user-dao.js`. Every handler reached by a route was read (`session.js`, `profile.js`, `allocations.js`, `benefits.js`, `contributions.js`, `memos.js`, `research.js`, `tutorial.js`, `error.js`, and the corresponding `*-dao.js` files) to see what each does with request input before it is trusted.
8: 
9: `semgrep --version` printed `1.177.0`, so semgrep ran: `semgrep --config <local pack> --config p/owasp-top-ten --metrics off --json /root/targets/NodeGoat` (29 findings from 113 rules over 72 tracked files). Every semgrep hit was read as a pointer, not taken as a finding on its own — in particular the `express-cookie-session-no-httponly` hit on `server.js:78-102` was checked against `express-session`'s own documented default (`cookie.httpOnly` defaults to `true`), which is why that specific hit is *not* reported as a finding: the codebase's own gap is the missing `maxAge` and `secure`, not `httpOnly`, and only the former is reported below with the line actually read. The `dsh-eval-on-input` hit on `app/routes/contributions.js` (an `eval()` on request body fields) and the `express-open-redirect` hit on `app/routes/index.js:72` are real but are injection-department findings, not access-department findings, and are named here only under "what was not covered".
10: 
11: ## Route table (application routes only; `/tutorial` is a static content router with no data access and was read but produced no findings)
12: 
13: | Method | Path | Middleware chain (as registered) | Unauthenticated caller | Wrong-identity authenticated caller |
14: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
15: | GET | `/` | none | 200, public welcome page | same |
16: | GET/POST | `/login` | none | 200 / processes login | same (public by design) |
17: | GET/POST | `/signup` | none | 200 / creates account | same (public by design) |
18: | GET | `/logout` | none | destroys session, redirects | same (public by design) |
19: | GET | `/dashboard` | `isLoggedIn` | redirected to `/login` | 200, own data only |
20: | GET/POST | `/profile` | `isLoggedIn` | redirected | 200 / **updates own record, no CSRF token checked — see finding** |
21: | GET/POST | `/contributions` | `isLoggedIn` | redirected | 200, own data only |
22: | GET | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | redirected | **200 — see finding: no `isAdmin` check** |
23: | POST | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | redirected | **succeeds, arbitrary target user — see finding** |
24: | GET | `/allocations/:userId` | `isLoggedIn` **only** | redirected | **200, returns the requested user's data regardless of caller identity — see finding** |
25: | GET/POST | `/memos` | `isLoggedIn` | redirected | 200 — memos are an intentionally shared company resource in this app, not a per-user record |
26: | GET | `/learn` | `isLoggedIn` | redirected | 200, open redirect (injection-department finding, not authorization) |
27: | GET | `/research` | `isLoggedIn` | redirected | 200 (SSRF via `needle.get`, injection-department finding) |
28: 
29: ## Findings
30: 
31: Eight findings, all `confidence: confirmed` — each is the result of reading the cited route's full middleware chain and the handler(s) it calls, not a pattern match. Full detail, evidence and fix are in `findings/access.json`; summarised here:
32: 
33: 1. **`access-idor-allocations`** (high, CWE-639) — `GET /allocations/:userId` (`app/routes/index.js:63`) checks only that *someone* is logged in; the handler trusts `req.params.userId` with no ownership check, and a commented-out line in the same file shows the intended fix (read from `req.session` instead) was never applied.
34: 2. **`access-missing-role-benefits-get`** (medium, CWE-862) — `GET /benefits` (`app/routes/index.js:55`) is missing the `isAdmin` middleware that is defined two lines above it and used nowhere. Any logged-in employee can list every other employee's benefits record.
35: 3. **`access-missing-role-benefits-post`** (critical, CWE-862) — `POST /benefits` (`app/routes/index.js:56`) has the same missing `isAdmin` check, and the handler additionally takes the target `userId` from the request body, so any logged-in user can rewrite any other user's `benefitStartDate` — a combined vertical (admin action) and horizontal (arbitrary target) authorization failure.
36: 4. **`access-session-fixation-login`** (medium, CWE-384) — `POST /login` (`app/routes/index.js:34`) sets `req.session.userId` without first calling `req.session.regenerate()`, unlike the signup handler in the same file which does. The session id issued before login survives login.
37: 5. **`access-csrf-profile-update`** (high, CWE-352) — `POST /profile` (`app/routes/index.js:48`) changes bank account/routing and SSN fields using only the session cookie for authentication. `csurf` is a declared dependency and the view even renders a hidden `_csrf` field, but the middleware that would mount it and populate `req.csrfToken()` is entirely commented out in `server.js:104-113`, so no request is ever checked.
38: 6. **`access-no-rate-limit-login`** (medium, CWE-307) — `POST /login` (`app/routes/index.js:34`) has no rate-limiting or lockout middleware in its chain, and `server.js`'s full middleware list confirms none is mounted application-wide either.
39: 7. **`access-timing-unsafe-password-compare`** (low, CWE-208) — the active password check in `app/data/user-dao.js:61` is `fromDB === fromUser`, a short-circuiting string comparison; the constant-time `bcrypt.compareSync` alternative is present in a comment but disabled.
40: 8. **`access-session-no-absolute-expiry`** (low, CWE-613) — the `session()` call in `server.js:78-85` has no `cookie` block at all, so no `maxAge` is ever set; only an explicit `/logout` ends a session, confirmed by a repo-wide search for `maxAge`.
41: 
42: ## What was not covered
43: 
44: - **JWT.** This application uses `express-session` server-side sessions exclusively; no JWT issuance or verification code exists anywhere in the tree, so the JWT-pitfalls checks in the `access` skill do not apply and were not exercised.
45: - **MFA.** No MFA/OTP code path exists in the application; not applicable.
46: - **`app/routes/tutorial.js`** and everything under `app/views/tutorial/` were read but are static lesson pages with no data access of their own; they were not analysed as attack surface beyond confirming they register no additional authenticated routes.
47: - **Injection-class findings visible in the same files** (the `eval()` on `contributions.js:32-34`, the open redirect at `index.js:72`, the SSRF-shaped fetch in `research.js:15-16`) were read but are out of scope for this department and are left for the injection department; they are not included in `findings/access.json`.
48: - **Secrets-class findings** — the hardcoded `cookieSecret` in `config/env/all.js:8` (the exact example used in this program's own `REPORTING.md`) was read and confirmed but is left for the secrets department rather than duplicated here.
49: - **Data-at-rest / password storage strength** (plaintext password storage, `user-dao.js:25`, with `bcrypt.hashSync` commented out at line 29) is closely related to finding 7 above but is a distinct CWE-916 concern; it was read and is mentioned in finding 7's evidence for context but is not filed as a separate finding here since the `data` department owns password-storage parameters per the skill catalog.
50: - **Runtime/deployment behaviour** — whether a reverse proxy, WAF, or infrastructure-level rate limiter sits in front of this app in production cannot be determined from a static read of this tree; findings 5 and 6 assume the application is reached directly, as `server.js`'s own `http.createServer(app).listen(port, ...)` (line 145) suggests it is designed to be.
51: - **`test/security/profile-test.js`** was opened only far enough to confirm it references `_csrf` as an empty field in its own requests (consistent with finding 5); it was not otherwise reviewed as it is test code, not application surface.

(End of file - total 51 lines)
</content>

41: - **`data-hardcoded-cookie-secret`** (`config/env/all.js:8`, CWE-798, critical,
42:   confirmed) — the express-session signing secret is the literal
43:   `"session_cookie_secret_key_here"`, committed in a public repository and used
44:   unmodified by `server.js`'s `session({ secret: cookieSecret, ... })`. Anyone
45:   who reads the source can forge a session cookie for any userId, including an
46:   admin, and authenticate as them with no credentials.

49:   high, confirmed) — `addUser()` stores the signup password unhashed; the
50:   bcrypt call that would fix it is present only as a comment, and
51:   `validateLogin`'s `comparePassword` does a bare `===` against the stored
52:   value, which only works if it is the plaintext password. A database
53:   compromise (or an unrelated bug that leaks the `users` collection) recovers
54:   every user's real password.

93:   rather than `confirmed`.

96: 
97: - **NoSQL/SSRF/XSS/ReDoS/eval injection** in `app/routes/contributions.js`

1: # Dependencies department — OWASP NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## What was looked at
4: 
5: The manifest, `package.json` at the target root, was read in full: 16 `dependencies` entries (lines 7-24) and 20 `devDependencies` entries (lines 41-61). Every declared version range was written down before any tool ran.
6: 
7: A lockfile is present (`package-lock.json`, `lockfileVersion: 2`), so `npm audit --json` was run inside the target (`/root/targets/NodeGoat`) rather than relying on the manifest's ranges alone — the target is read-only and `npm audit` only reads the tree and queries the registry; it wrote nothing into it. **The registry was reachable**: the audit returned real advisory data (145 total findings across `prod`+`dev`+`optional`, broken out by severity as `critical: 38, high: 66, moderate: 33, low: 8`), not a network error, so this report is not a declared-versions-only fallback. Registry lookups (`npm view <pkg> time`, `npm view <pkg> deprecated`, `npm view <pkg> version`) were also reachable and were used to check maintenance status and to confirm the currently-published latest version for several packages; these are read-only registry queries, not installs. `npm audit fix --dry-run` was run once to see the tool's own remediation graph; `--dry-run` performs no writes and none were made — nothing was installed or modified in the target tree at any point.
8: 
9: `semgrep --version` reported `1.177.0`. Semgrep's rules are aimed at code-pattern vulnerabilities (injection, XSS sinks, auth logic), not at dependency-manifest review, and were not the tool this department's task called for; no semgrep pass was run for this department, since the task specifies `npm audit` as the tool for this review and semgrep hits would only be "a place to read," not a dependency finding in themselves.
10: 
11: Every direct dependency npm audit flagged as vulnerable was traced back to its manifest line and its resolved lockfile version. Where a package carried no advisory but showed clear signs of abandonment, the npm registry's own metadata (last publish date, `deprecated` field) was read directly rather than assumed.
12: 
13: ## What was found
14: 
15: 11 findings, grouped by the direct dependency that pulls the advisories in rather than one finding per transitive package:
16: 
17: - **critical (3)**: `underscore@1.9.1` (declared `^1.8.3`, `package.json:23`) has a known arbitrary-code-execution advisory (GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq, CWE-94) plus an unbounded-recursion DoS, 2 distinct advisories on the package itself. `swig@1.4.2` (declared `^1.4.2`, `package.json:22`) has an unpatched arbitrary local file read (GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6, CWE-22) and is itself abandoned — 1.4.2 (2014) is still the newest version the registry has ever published, and the registry marks it `deprecated: "This package is no longer maintained"`, so `fixAvailable` is `false`: there is no in-range upgrade. `forever@2.0.0` (declared `^2.0.0`, `package.json:15`), the process supervisor the app's own start path uses, pulls in `nconf`'s prototype-pollution advisory (GHSA-6xwr-q98w-rvg7) through `flatiron`/`forever-monitor`; fixing it needs a major-version jump to `forever@4.0.3`.
18: - **high (5)**: `mongodb@2.2.36` (DoS, GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r, plus 2 more via `mongodb-core`), `marked@0.3.5` (6 distinct XSS/ReDoS advisories, CWE-79/CWE-1333, on a version pinned exactly since 2015), `body-parser@1.18.3` (URL-encoding DoS, GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7, CWE-405, plus 6 more via `qs`), `express@4.16.4` (open redirect and reflected-XSS-via-redirect on the framework itself, plus 6 bundled dependencies — `body-parser`, `cookie`, `path-to-regexp`, `qs`, `send`, `serve-static` — for 16 distinct advisories reachable through this one direct dependency), and `helmet@2.3.0` (no advisory on helmet's own code, but its `connect`→`debug` chain carries a ReDoS and `helmet-csp` carries a CSP configuration-override advisory).
19: - **low (1)**: `bcrypt-nodejs@0.0.3` (declared `0.0.3` pinned, `package.json:8`) — the package doing the application's password hashing. No CVE/GHSA is open against it, so this is a maintenance finding, not a vulnerability finding: the registry itself returns `deprecated: "bcrypt-nodejs is no longer actively maintained. Please use bcrypt or bcryptjs."`, and its final release was published 2013-02-25.
20: - **info (2)**: `node-esapi@0.0.1` (`package.json:20`) has had exactly one release, ever, published 2014-01-31 — a maintenance finding, not a vulnerability finding, since no advisory exists. A grouped finding at the `devDependencies` block (`package.json:41`) covers 14 flagged dev-only packages (`async`, `cypress`, `grunt` and 5 of its plugins, `jshint`, `mocha`, `nodemon`, `selenium-webdriver`, `zaproxy`) whose transitive trees carry 105 distinct advisories between them, concentrated in `cypress` (43), `grunt-npm-install` (54, heavily overlapping with `grunt`'s own 16), and `zaproxy` (31). None of these ship in the production dependency tree; the risk is to the build/CI environment, not the deployed application, so this stays `info`.
21: 
22: Every finding names the manifest line, the exact `package.json` snippet, the declared range, the resolved lockfile version, and the advisory identifier(s) with their own CWE where the advisory itself states one. Fixed versions are stated from the audit's own `fixAvailable` data (including where it demands a SemVer-major bump) or, for `swig`, the absence of any fix.
23: 
24: ## What was not covered
25: 
26: - **Every other transitive package `npm audit` flagged was not written up as its own finding.** The audit's `vulnerabilities` map lists far more than the 24 direct packages summarized above; per the department's grouping rule, only the direct dependency each advisory chain enters through is cited, with the transitive count stated in that finding's evidence rather than as separate findings. Two low-severity advisories seen but not written up individually: `cookie` (GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x, via both `csurf` and `express-session`) and `on-headers` (GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q, via `express-session`) — both low severity and already represented under the `express` finding's bundled-dependency count.
27: - **Typosquatting was not checked.** Every declared package name was read but not individually compared against a known-package edit-distance list; nothing in the 16 production or 20 dev names looked like a plausible typosquat during this read, but that is an impression, not a check this report claims to have run.
28: - **Pinned-vs-floating review was not written up as its own findings.** Several security-sensitive packages (`bcrypt-nodejs`, `marked`, `needle`, `node-esapi`) are pinned to exact versions rather than ranges, which is protective against drift but is also why they never pick up a patched release automatically; this is noted here rather than as a separate finding since it is the same underlying fact as the version-currency findings above, not a distinct risk.
29: - **`Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` base-image pinning were read but not reviewed for platform/CI dependency risk** — that is this codebase's `platform` department's remit, not `dependencies`'s.
30: - **Runtime/production behavior of any advisory was not tested.** This review is a static reading of the manifest, the lockfile, and the registry's own advisory and metadata feeds; no exploit was attempted against a running instance of NodeGoat.
31: - **No findings were dropped by the examiner.** `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/dependencies.json` passed clean on the first corrected run (11 of 11 findings verified); nothing in this department's set needed to be disclosed as dropped.

(End of file - total 31 lines)

67:   on every process start with no redaction and no `NODE_ENV` guard, widening exposure from
68:   "whoever reads the source" to "whoever reads the process/container logs."
69: 
70: - **`secrets-006-zap-api-key`** (`config/env/development.js:6`, CWE-798, low, confirmed) — a
71:   hardcoded OWASP ZAP proxy API key, confirmed as a live credential used by
72:   `test/security/profile-test.js` against a private (RFC1918) ZAP host. Lower severity because it
73:   is development/test tooling, not a production application secret, and the target host is not
74:   internet-reachable by default.
75: 
76: - **`secrets-007-e2e-fixture-admin-password`** (`test/e2e/fixtures/users/admin.json:3`, CWE-798,
77:   **info**, confirmed) — the same default admin password is duplicated in a Cypress test fixture,
78:   consumed by `test/e2e/integration/login_spec.js`. Reported at the lowest severity of the group,
79:   and explicitly noted in its evidence as a test-fixture duplicate rather than the primary source
80:   of exposure, which is `secrets-002`.
81: 
82: ## What was not covered
83: 
84: - The `.git` history was not scanned for secrets that may have been rotated out of the current
85:   tree (e.g. with gitleaks/trufflehog over full history); this review only read the files as they
86:   exist in the locked tree.
87: - `node_modules` and third-party vendored assets (`app/assets/vendor/**`) were not audited for
88:   embedded credentials; they are vendored libraries, not this project's own configuration.
89: - `package-lock.json` was not read line-by-line for embedded registry tokens; a targeted grep found
90:   none, but the file is large (dependency review is a separate department's remit).
91: - Binary/image assets (`app/assets/images/*.png`, `favicon.ico`, font files) were not opened; they
92:   are not credential-shaped and are outside this department's grep patterns.
93: - Runtime behavior — what value `MONGODB_URI`, `PORT`, or `NODE_ENV` actually hold in any real
94:   deployment of this app — was not checked; only the source-committed defaults were read, since no
95:   running deployment was available to this review.
96: - `artifacts/cert/server.crt` was confirmed to exist and begin `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----` but
97:   its full contents were not read; it is the public half of the key pair reported in
98:   `secrets-004` and carries no additional secret.
99: - This review did not attempt to determine whether `artifacts/cert/server.key` and
100:   `artifacts/cert/server.crt` are a matching pair by cryptographic verification (e.g. comparing
101:   moduli); the finding does not depend on that and treats the key as sensitive regardless.

(End of file - total 101 lines)
</content>

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: // Mechanical examiner of a code-safety report. It is in the report
3: // repository's base commit, so no department can change what measures it.
4: //
5: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path>  one department's findings
6: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path> --list-invalid
7: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --report           the merged report
8: //
9: // `--findings` decides one findings file against the target tree. Adding
10: // `--list-invalid` turns the same decision into a report: the failing ids go to
11: // stdout, one per line, and the exit code is 0, which is how the integration
12: // learns which findings to drop and disclose.
13: //
14: // `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
15: // disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
16: // findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.
17: //
18: // Exit 0 only when every rule holds; otherwise every failure is printed to
19: // stderr, one per line, and the exit code is 1. Node built-ins only, because
20: // this runs in a worktree that installs nothing.
21: import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
22: import { existsSync, readdirSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
23: import { basename, join, relative, resolve } from 'node:path'
24: 
25: /** Severities a finding may claim, most severe first. */
26: const SEVERITIES = ['critical', 'high', 'medium', 'low', 'info']
27: 
28: /** How sure a finding's author is that the cited code is exploitable as described. */
29: const CONFIDENCES = ['confirmed', 'likely', 'possible']
30: 
31: /** Sections SAFETY-REPORT.md carries, in this order. */
32: const SECTIONS = [
33:   '## Résumé exécutif',
34:   '## Executive summary',
35:   '## Scope and method',
36:   '## Findings',
37:   '## What was not covered',
38:   '## Certificate',
39: ]
40: 
41: /** The claim the certificate must make verbatim, and the only claim this review supports. */
42: const HONESTY = 'This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".'
43: 
44: /** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */
45: const OVERCLAIMS = /\bno vulnerabilities\b|\bfree of vulnerabilities\b|\b(?:is|are|was|were) secure\b|\bsafe to deploy\b|\bproven secure\b|\bfully audited\b/i
46: 
47: /** Text a report still carrying its template is refused for. */
48: const PLACEHOLDER = /\bTODO\b|\bTBD\b|\bFIXME\b|lorem ipsum|<placeholder>|PLACEHOLDER/i
49: 
50: /** String fields every finding states in prose. */
51: const PROSE_FIELDS = ['title', 'evidence', 'impact', 'fix']
52: 
53: /** How a file's text is compared with a finding's quoted snippet. */
54: const normalize = (text) => text.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()
55: 
56: /** Lowercase hex SHA-256 of one buffer or string. */
57: const sha256 = (content) => createHash('sha256').update(content).digest('hex')
58: 
59: /**
60:  * Every file under one directory, relative and sorted, skipping the excluded names.
61:  * @param {string} root directory to walk
62:  * @param {string[]} exclude directory basenames never descended into
63:  * @returns {string[]} relative POSIX-ish paths, sorted
64:  */
65: function walk(root, exclude) {
66:   const found = []
67:   const descend = (directory) => {
68:     for (const entry of readdirSync(directory, { withFileTypes: true }).sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
69:       const path = join(directory, entry.name)
70:       if (entry.isDirectory()) {
71:         if (!exclude.includes(entry.name)) descend(path)
72:       } else if (entry.isFile()) found.push(relative(root, path))
73:     }
74:   }
75:   descend(root)
76:   return found.sort()
77: }
78: 
79: /** One target tree as the lock and the verifier both read it: the files, their digests, and their text. */
80: class Target {
81:   /**
82:    * @param {string} reportRoot the report repository the lock is committed in
83:    * @param {string[]} failures collector every rule appends to
84:    */
85:   constructor(reportRoot, failures) {
86:     this.failures = failures
87:     this.root = undefined
88:     this.files = new Map()
89:     this.lines = new Map()
90:     const lockPath = join(reportRoot, 'target.json')
91:     if (!existsSync(lockPath)) {
92:       failures.push('target.json is missing from this worktree; the base commit carries the lock of the tree under review')
93:       return
94:     }
95:     const lock = JSON.parse(readFileSync(lockPath, 'utf8'))
96:     this.root = lock.root
97:     this.exclude = lock.exclude ?? []
98:     this.digest = lock.sha256
99:     for (const [path, hash] of Object.entries(lock.files)) this.files.set(path, hash)
100:     this.checkTree()
101:   }
102: 
103:   /**
104:    * Refuse a target that changed since the base commit locked it: a finding
105:    * cites a line of the tree this program was asked to review, and a tree a
106:    * department edited is no longer that tree.
107:    */
108:   checkTree() {
109:     if (!existsSync(this.root)) {
110:       this.failures.push(`the target tree ${this.root} is not on this host, so no citation can be resolved`)
111:       this.root = undefined
112:       return
113:     }
114:     const present = walk(this.root, this.exclude)
115:     for (const path of present) {
116:       if (!this.files.has(path)) this.failures.push(`the target tree gained ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
117:     }
118:     for (const [path, hash] of this.files) {
119:       if (!present.includes(path)) {
120:         this.failures.push(`the target tree lost ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
121:         continue
122:       }
123:       if (sha256(readFileSync(join(this.root, path))) !== hash) {
124:         this.failures.push(`the target tree's ${path} changed since the base commit locked it; the target is read-only for this program`)
125:       }
126:     }
127:   }
128: 
129:   /**
130:    * The lines of one target file.
131:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
132:    * @returns {string[] | undefined} the file's lines, or undefined when it is not in the locked tree
133:    */
134:   linesOf(path) {
135:     if (this.root === undefined || !this.files.has(path)) return undefined
136:     if (!this.lines.has(path)) this.lines.set(path, readFileSync(join(this.root, path), 'utf8').split('\n'))
137:     return this.lines.get(path)
138:   }
139: 
140:   /**
141:    * Whether one `file:line` citation resolves in the locked tree.
142:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
143:    * @param {number} line 1-based line number
144:    * @returns {boolean} whether the file is under review and holds that line
145:    */
146:   resolves(path, line) {
147:     const lines = this.linesOf(path)
148:     return lines !== undefined && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lines.length
149:   }
150: }
151: 
152: /**
153:  * Decide one finding against the target tree.
154:  * @param {unknown} finding one entry of a findings file
155:  * @param {number} index its position, named when the entry has no usable id
156:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the finding cites
157:  * @param {Set<string>} seen ids already used in this file
158:  * @returns {string[]} every rule this finding broke, empty when it holds
159:  */
160: function checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen) {
161:   const failures = []
162:   if (finding === null || typeof finding !== 'object' || Array.isArray(finding)) {
163:     return [`finding #${index + 1} is not a JSON object`]
164:   }
165:   const id = finding.id
166:   const name = typeof id === 'string' && id !== '' ? id : `#${index + 1}`
167:   const fail = (rule) => void failures.push(`${name}: ${rule}`)
168:   // Letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`: wide enough for both the `SEC-001`
169:   // numbering the knowledge pack's schema uses and a department-prefixed name.
170:   if (typeof id !== 'string' || !/^[A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*$/.test(id)) fail('id must be letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores')
171:   else if (seen.has(id)) fail('id is used twice in this file')
172:   else seen.add(id)
173:   if (typeof finding.cwe !== 'string' || !/^CWE-\d+$/.test(finding.cwe)) fail('cwe must match CWE-<number>')
174:   if (typeof finding.owasp !== 'string' || finding.owasp.trim() === '') fail('owasp must name the category')
175:   if (!SEVERITIES.includes(finding.severity)) fail(`severity must be one of ${SEVERITIES.join(', ')}`)
176:   if (!CONFIDENCES.includes(finding.confidence)) fail(`confidence must be one of ${CONFIDENCES.join(', ')}`)
177:   for (const field of PROSE_FIELDS) {
178:     if (typeof finding[field] !== 'string' || finding[field].trim() === '') fail(`${field} must be a non-empty string`)
179:   }
180:   if (!Array.isArray(finding.references) || finding.references.some(reference => typeof reference !== 'string')) {
181:     fail('references must be an array of strings')
182:   }
183:   const { file, line, endLine, snippet } = finding
184:   if (typeof file !== 'string' || file === '' || file.startsWith('/') || file.split('/').includes('..')) {
185:     fail('file must be a path relative to the target root')
186:     return failures
187:   }
188:   const lines = target.linesOf(file)
189:   if (lines === undefined) {
190:     fail(`file ${file} is not in the tree under review`)
191:     return failures
192:   }
193:   if (!Number.isInteger(line) || line < 1 || line > lines.length) {
194:     fail(`line ${JSON.stringify(line)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
195:     return failures
196:   }
197:   const last = endLine === undefined ? line : endLine
198:   if (!Number.isInteger(last) || last < line || last > lines.length) {
199:     fail(`endLine ${JSON.stringify(endLine)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
200:     return failures
201:   }
202:   if (typeof snippet !== 'string' || snippet.trim() === '') {
203:     fail('snippet must quote the cited line')
204:     return failures
205:   }
206:   const quoted = normalize(lines.slice(line - 1, last).join('\n'))
207:   if (normalize(snippet) !== quoted) {
208:     fail(`snippet does not match ${file}:${line}, which reads ${JSON.stringify(quoted.slice(0, 160))}`)
209:   }
210:   return failures
211: }
212: 
213: /**
214:  * Read one findings file.
215:  * @param {string} path the file to read
216:  * @param {string[]} failures collector a malformed file is reported on
217:  * @returns {unknown[]} the entries, empty when the file is missing or malformed
218:  */
219: function readFindings(path, failures) {
220:   if (!existsSync(path)) {
221:     failures.push(`${path} is missing`)
222:     return []
223:   }
224:   let parsed
225:   try {
226:     parsed = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'))
227:   } catch (error) {
228:     failures.push(`${path} is not JSON: ${error.message}`)
229:     return []
230:   }
231:   if (!Array.isArray(parsed)) {
232:     failures.push(`${path} must be a JSON array of findings`)
233:     return []
234:   }
235:   return parsed
236: }
237: 
238: /**
239:  * Decide one findings file on its own.
240:  * @param {string} path the findings file
241:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree it cites
242:  * @returns {{ failures: string[], invalid: string[], findings: unknown[] }} the broken rules, the ids that broke them, and the entries
243:  */
244: function checkFindingsFile(path, target) {
245:   const failures = []
246:   const findings = readFindings(path, failures)
247:   const invalid = []
248:   const seen = new Set()
249:   findings.forEach((finding, index) => {
250:     const broken = checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen)
251:     if (broken.length === 0) return
252:     failures.push(...broken.map(rule => `${basename(path)}: ${rule}`))
253:     invalid.push(typeof finding?.id === 'string' ? finding.id : `#${index + 1}`)
254:   })
255:   return { failures, invalid, findings }
256: }
257: 
258: /**
259:  * The body of one section of the report.
260:  * @param {string} text the whole report
261:  * @param {string} heading the section heading, including its `##`
262:  * @returns {string} the text between this heading and the next one, empty when absent
263:  */
264: function section(text, heading) {
265:   const start = text.indexOf(`${heading}\n`)
266:   if (start === -1) return ''
267:   const body = text.slice(start + heading.length + 1)
268:   const next = body.search(/^## /m)
269:   return next === -1 ? body : body.slice(0, next)
270: }
271: 
272: /**
273:  * Decide SAFETY-REPORT.md, findings.json and the disclosure of what was dropped.
274:  * @param {string} root the report repository
275:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the report cites
276:  * @returns {string[]} every rule the report broke
277:  */
278: function checkReport(root, target) {
279:   const reportPath = join(root, 'SAFETY-REPORT.md')
280:   if (!existsSync(reportPath)) {
281:     return [`SAFETY-REPORT.md is missing; REPORTING.md in this worktree states the sections it carries: ${SECTIONS.join(', ')}`]
282:   }
283:   const text = readFileSync(reportPath, 'utf8')
284:   const failures = []
285:   let previous = -1
286:   for (const heading of SECTIONS) {
287:     const at = text.indexOf(`${heading}\n`)
288:     if (at === -1) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md has no section ${JSON.stringify(heading)}`)
289:     else if (at < previous) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md has ${JSON.stringify(heading)} out of order; the order is ${SECTIONS.join(' then ')}`)
290:     else previous = at
291:   }
292:   const placeholder = PLACEHOLDER.exec(text)
293:   if (placeholder !== null) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md still carries placeholder text: ${JSON.stringify(placeholder[0])}`)
294:   const overclaim = OVERCLAIMS.exec(text)
295:   if (overclaim !== null) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md claims more than this review supports: ${JSON.stringify(overclaim[0])}`)
296: 
297:   const union = checkFindingsFile(join(root, 'findings.json'), target)
298:   failures.push(...union.failures)
299:   const findings = union.findings.filter(finding => typeof finding?.id === 'string')
300: 
301:   const keys = new Set()
302:   for (const finding of findings) {
303:     const key = `${finding.file}:${finding.line}:${finding.cwe}`
304:     if (keys.has(key)) failures.push(`findings.json states ${key} twice; the union is deduplicated by file, line and cwe`)
305:     keys.add(key)
306:   }
307: 
308:   const listed = section(text, '## Findings')
309:   for (const finding of findings) {
310:     if (!listed.includes(finding.id)) failures.push(`the Findings section does not cite ${finding.id}`)
311:   }
312:   // The lookbehind keeps a URL's `host:port` out of the citation vocabulary:
313:   // the host is preceded by a slash, so no citation ever starts there.
314:   for (const [, path, line] of text.matchAll(/(?<![\w/.\-])([\w.-]+(?:\/[\w.-]+)*\.\w+):(\d+)\b/g)) {
315:     if (!target.resolves(path, Number(line))) failures.push(`the citation ${path}:${line} does not resolve in the tree under review`)
316:   }
317: 
318:   const counts = Object.fromEntries(SEVERITIES.map(severity => [severity, findings.filter(finding => finding.severity === severity).length]))
319:   for (const heading of ['## Résumé exécutif', '## Executive summary']) {
320:     const body = section(text, heading)
321:     for (const severity of SEVERITIES) {
322:       const stated = new RegExp(`^- ${severity}: (\\d+)$`, 'm').exec(body)
323:       if (stated === null) failures.push(`${heading} does not state a "- ${severity}: <count>" line`)
324:       else if (Number(stated[1]) !== counts[severity]) {
325:         failures.push(`${heading} states ${severity}: ${stated[1]}, and findings.json holds ${counts[severity]}`)
326:       }
327:     }
328:   }
329: 
330:   const uncovered = section(text, '## What was not covered')
